questions.q: Identify the two question types: "What reason does Manjula give for writing her novel in English?" and "Why does the playwright make Manjula's Image challenge her account of Malini's illness?" Label each as literal or inferential.
questions.a: First question is literal (text states: "it burst out in English... surprised even me"). Second is inferential (requires analyzing the Image's function as Manjula's suppressed conscience). A wrong answer labels both literal — revealing the student cannot distinguish explicit retrieval from implicit analysis, a fatal error in CBSE 3-6 mark questions where inferential depth carries 60% weightage.

questions.q: A student writes: "Manjula is selfish because she didn't move to Koramangala after her parents died." Using only the text, explain why this is an incomplete inference and what textual evidence complicates it.
questions.a: The inference ignores Manjula's stated reasons: job proximity, house maintenance burden, and Malini's own insistence on selling Koramangala ("she wouldn't listen... wanted no sacrifices"). A student missing this treats characters as flat — a Class 12 error where CBSE expects recognition of dramatic irony (Manjula's defensive tone vs. Malini's agency). The correct response cites Malini's dialogue: "She adjusted beautifully to the smaller house."

questions.q: Apply the PEEL structure to answer: "How does the Announcer's introduction establish the central conflict of language politics before Manjula speaks?" Provide Point, Evidence (quote), Explanation, Link.
questions.a: Point: The Announcer frames Manjula's English novel as "betrayal" of Kannada. Evidence: "stunned the world... by writing a novel... in English!" and "how many of our Kannada writers are lecturers in English." Explanation: The contrast between "Kannada writers... lecturers in English" and Manjula's "bestseller all over the world" sets up the tension between linguistic loyalty and global success. Link: This prefigures Manjula's defence ("A writer seeks audiences where she can find them") and the Akademi President's attack. A wrong answer paraphrases without quoting — losing 1-2 marks for missing "textual evidence" requirement in CBSE marking scheme.

questions.q: Analyze how the stage direction "The red light switches off. She smiles contentedly. Whew! That'll get them. Good. I have taken enough shit from them" transforms a literal comprehension of Manjula's mood into an inferential reading of her public vs. private self.
questions.a: Literal: Manjula is relieved the broadcast ended. Inferential: The private vulgarity ("shit") and vengeful satisfaction ("That'll get them") contradict her public grace ("Namaskara... Good Night"). The stage direction is the only window into her unperformed self — a structural device Karnad uses to prepare the Image's entrance. A student answering only "she is happy" misses the irony central to the play's satire on celebrity performance.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The Image is merely a technical glitch, not a dramatic device." Defend or refute using three pieces of textual evidence from the play's second half.
questions.a: Refute. Evidence 1: Image knows private details ("Her illness was unfortunate... she got the best of everything") no broadcast could capture. Evidence 2: Image analyses Manjula's psychology ("You wouldn't have been as bright") — a glitch cannot interpret motive. Evidence 3: The dialogue structure (Manjula: "Who are you?" Image: "Me? You.") confirms the Image is her externalized conscience. A student accepting the "glitch" reading fails the play's central metaphor: the Image IS the broken reflection of Manjula's fragmented identity — a CUET/NEET-style conceptual trap testing symbolic literacy.

questions.q: Create a 40-word inferential question on the Pramod-Malini-Manjula triangle that cannot be answered by a single direct quote, and write its model answer using two separate textual references.
questions.a: Question: "What does Pramod's absence during the novel's US launch reveal about the emotional architecture of Manjula's success?" Model Answer: Pramod's email congratulations from Los Angeles without attending ("Apologised that he couldn't get leave") and Manjula's admission "He didn't even hint at it" suggest his software career now mirrors the English-language success that separated Manjula from her Kannada roots — both are migrations Malini (who "breathed, laughed, dreamt in English") embodied but Manjula performs. A poor answer cites only the email, missing the structural parallel.
